extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of architectural history, art criticism, and design who are evaluating or interpreting Byzantine and Gothic architecture (esp. Venetian examples).
extracted.subtask_description: Formulate criteria for recognizing, interpreting, and judging Byzantine and Gothic architecture (with emphasis on Venetian examples), including both external forms and underlying mental/aesthetic elements. The guidance explains how to read ornament, color, symbolism, and structural/expressive features to assess a building's 'Gothicness' or Byzantine character.

rubrics_metrics.name: System of grounding with gold and color (Byzantine mosaic grounds)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of a golden ground formed of glass mosaic inserted in the hollows of the marble, each glass square having leaf-gold on its surface protected by another thin film of glass so its lustre resists time and weather.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the visual effect of reflective golden mosaic grounds against white or veined marble: in shadow the golden surface shows bright behind dark traceries; in sunlight, white sculpture appears as snowy tracery on a golden ground. Note that neglected mosaic may disappear with weathering, so absence is not proof it never existed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of colored/veined marble and selective gilding in palaces
rubrics_metrics.description: Shafts and facings were of veined or variously colored marble while capitals and sculptures were often pure white marble relieved upon the veined ground, or (more probably in richer palaces) grounded with gold mosaic and in inferior ones with blue color; only leaves and edges of sculpture gilded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing decorative effect, look for contrast between veined/colorful architectural surfaces and pale sculptural relief; consider restoration history (mosaic often removed for reuse) when interpreting surviving material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of colored bands and inlaid disks as Eastern-derived ornament
rubrics_metrics.description: Bands of deeper color (generally alternate russet and green) in archivolts and circular disks of green serpentine and porphyry were characteristic ornaments, especially grateful to the Eastern mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize such repetitive color bands and inlaid circular disks as intentional chromatic motifs with Eastern provenance; consider their placement and alternation when judging stylistic lineage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Figurative and symbolic sculpture (Christian iconography)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sculptural subjects often carry Christian symbolism: the cross as a principal ornament, the peacock as symbol of resurrection (sometimes depicted drinking from a fountain or font as a baptismal type), the vine as a type of Christ or of union with him, the dove as the Comforter, and contending animals as references to powers of evil.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret sculptural motifs in light of early Christian symbolism; read repeated animal/plant motifs as theological or devotional signs rather than mere decorative subjects, but avoid over-insisting on occult meanings where context is ambiguous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Color as a sacred and moral element
rubrics_metrics.description: Color is not merely decorative or sensual pleasure but 'the holiest, the most divine, the most solemn' of visual gifts; all good color has a pensiveness and purity that aligns with thoughtful and pious minds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge color schemes by their moral/aesthetic tone: pure, pensive hues signal nobleness and spiritual seriousness; bright/gay color alone should not be equated with frivolity. Consider cultural and religious contexts that sanctify certain hues (e.g., purple, blue, gold).

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation of a painter's (or builder's) moral/religious character to quality of color
rubrics_metrics.description: A more faithful and earnest religion in a painter produces purer and more prevalent color; conversely, irreligious or sensual dispositions tend to produce cold, gloomy, and valueless colouring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When attributing aesthetic qualities, consider biographical or cultural evidence about the artist's temper or religious seriousness as influencing chromatic choices (examples: Frà Angelico's pure coloring vs Salvator Rosa's gloomy tones).

rubrics_metrics.name: Universal law: pure color correlates with noble thought
rubrics_metrics.description: Across traditions, early religious painting and sacred architecture tend to be brilliant in hue and holy in thought, while later or licentious schools tend toward cold paleness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the presence of vibrant, harmonious coloring as one indicator of spiritual or intellectual ambition in a work; contrast with paleness or monochrome as signs of different cultural priorities (e.g., Renaissance luxury vs earlier sacred colorfulness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Gothicness as a composite quality (external forms + internal elements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Gothic character is not any single form (pointed arches, vaults, flying buttresses, grotesques) but the union of external forms and internal mental elements; both material form and expressive mental tendencies must be present for a building to be truly Gothic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess buildings for degree of 'Gothicness' by checking both structural/formal features and the expressive/mental attributes (e.g., love of variety, naturalism). A building with only forms but lacking the internal spirit is not fully Gothic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gothicness is a matter of degree (degree-based assessment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every Gothic-period building differs; Gothicness is a variable quality—some buildings have more Gothic character, others less. It is the union and degree of constituent elements that produces Gothicness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a graduated evaluative approach rather than binary labeling: identify which Gothic elements are present and to what extent, and combine them to reach an overall judgment of purity or mixture of styles.

rubrics_metrics.name: External forms associated with Gothic
rubrics_metrics.description: Forms often counted Gothic include pointed arches, vaulted roofs, flying buttresses, and grotesque sculptures, but none of these alone constitutes Gothic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When cataloguing features, list canonical Gothic formal elements but avoid treating any single feature as definitive; examine how these forms interact and whether they are animated by Gothic mental expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental elements (primary): Savageness, Changefulness, Naturalism, Grotesqueness, Rigidity, Redundance
rubrics_metrics.description: The Gothic character's chief internal or moral elements (in order of importance) are: 1. Savageness, 2. Changefulness, 3. Naturalism, 4. Grotesqueness, 5. Rigidity, 6. Redundance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this list as the principal dimensions when diagnosing Gothic spirit: the presence, absence, or degree of each contributes to the building's overall Gothicness. The union of many of these elements gives stronger Gothic character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Savageness as a positive Gothic attribute
rubrics_metrics.description: Savageness (rudeness, wildness) denotes a noble, sturdy power and roughness of work that expresses the Northern character; it is not a defect but an essential dignity of Gothic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize rough, forceful, 'wolfish' energy, and irregular, rugged forms as legitimate expressions of Gothicness—view them as honest responses to climate, labor, and spiritual temperament rather than mere barbarism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three systems of ornament (servile, constitutional, revolutionary)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ornamental systems divide into: (1) Servile ornament—execution fully subordinated to a master with geometrical, perfectly symmetric designs; (2) Constitutional ornament—executive workmen have some independent will but acknowledge higher powers; (3) Revolutionary ornament—no executive inferiority admitted, full freedom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate ornamental practice by the degree of autonomy and individual expression permitted to craftsmen: servile ornament stresses rule-and-precision, constitutional ornament allows some artisan agency, and revolutionary ornament treats each executor as an independent creative force. Use this taxonomy to interpret stylistic intent and social/ religious values behind ornament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Christian/medieval ornament principle: recognition of individual imperfection and value
rubrics_metrics.description: Medieval Christian ornament abandons servile slavery of the workman, recognizing the individual's value and imperfection—exhorting each to 'do what you can, and confess frankly what you are unable to do.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging medieval ornament, look for signs that workmanship acknowledges human limitation and individuality (irregularities, local variations) as a moral/aesthetic virtue rather than a flaw; this underpins the constitutional or revolutionary modes of ornament.
